posts.text:
Most people do not have a LinkedIn problem.

They have a finishing problem.

They draft a sharp post, then rewrite it until it sounds like a keynote, then never hit publish.

The accounts that grow are usually not the cleverest. They are the ones that show up on a schedule with one useful idea, written the way they talk at work.

If you are waiting for a perfect week of content, you will still be waiting next quarter.

What is the post you have been sitting on?

Every other request we get is "just write a small custom module."

It is rarely small. We are the ones who have to upgrade it, explain it to the next consultant, and own it when Odoo moves a field in 19.0.

Last month a customer wanted a unique inventory workflow. The instinct on their side was development. Ours was: sit on our hands for a day and try the stock of settings first. A few configuration tweaks covered it. No extra module. No extra bill of materials for our maintenance calendar.

I would rather lose a customisation invoice than inherit a fork we cannot stand behind after the next upgrade.

We still write modules. We ship them when configuration actually cannot carry the process. The filter is simple: will we still be proud of this code after two version jumps?

When do you push back on a customisation that looks easy on paper?

#Configuration #Customization #Odoo #Inventory

I will not put an AI feature on one of our Odoo apps until I have seen the master data.

We tried anyway once. Invoice approvals, discrepancy flags, the whole demo-friendly stack. On paper it looked like we had a product. In production the vendor names disagreed with themselves, amounts had typos, and the model spent its intelligence shouting about duplicates that were just dirty records.

Our team spent more hours cleaning data than the assistant ever saved. That is on me. I shipped clever before I shipped boring.

Now the rule inside the company is blunt: clean the partners, products, and taxes first. Then we talk about models. A workflow that looks smart on top of a mess just scales the mess.

What is the first table you would refuse to automate until it is clean?

#AI #DataQuality #MasterData #Invoices

The AI invoice demo always looks finished. Vendor PDF in, Odoo bill out.

We built that path. Scan, extract, write the vendor bill. Then the real inbox showed up: twenty vendor layouts, half of them scans, a few with the tax in a footnote. The model filled fields. Our accountants spent the afternoon unscrewing them.

I stopped treating extraction as the product. The product is what we allow to hit posted data.

Now we only let AI draft. A person still owns the confirm. And we spend the money on vendor templates and master data before we spend it on another model.

I would rather ship a slower, trusted bill than a fast one we have to reverse on month-end.

Where do you still require a human confirm before anything writes into Odoo?

#AI #Invoices #DocumentAI #Automation

We treated a payment-gateway integration as a weekend job.

Collect the payment. Write the accounting. Happy path in the sandbox. Then live traffic arrived: paid in the gateway, not paid in Odoo, or the reverse. We owned both sides of that lie in front of the customer.

The bug was not the API. It was that "success" did not mean the same thing in both systems. Statuses, retries, partial captures — none of that was in the sales conversation.

We stopped, mapped every state, and wrote the boring document nobody wanted. That mapping is now the first artefact I ask for before we take an integration onto our plate.

I will not sell "it just syncs" again. If we cannot name the failure states, we are not ready to ship.

What status mismatch have you had to explain to a customer after go-live?

#Integrations #Payments #Odoo #Accounting

Migrations are critical, but they’re not as straightforward as they seem. I always start with the data. I check for completeness, accuracy, and any discrepancies that could lead to havoc post-migration.

Recently, we had a client who wanted to migrate from an outdated system to Odoo. The initial assessment looked promising — they showed us their database and it seemed tidy. We discovered later, during a deeper dive, that their SKU numbers were not standardized. Some were numeric, others alphanumeric, and it got worse with product categories.

If we had moved forward without addressing these issues, the migration would have failed. Products would be mismatched, inventory levels could be incorrect, and financial reporting would spiral into chaos. This taught us a lesson: don't just trust initial data presentations. Dig deeper to reveal hidden complexities.

What’s your go-to check before a migration? Any surprises you've encountered that changed your approach?

#Migration #Odoo #Inventory

We've all seen AI that drafts content. It's great for generating ideas or creating templates, but there's a hard line when it comes to allowing it to write directly into production data. Recently, we faced a scenario where a customer wanted to automate responses to support tickets using AI. The drafting AI could produce coherent replies, but when we considered letting it post directly to the ticketing system, I pushed back.

Here’s why: drafting doesn’t account for the nuances of each ticket. An AI can misinterpret context or misapply tone. It might suggest a resolution that doesn't fit due to missing background knowledge. I insisted we keep a manual review step before any AI-generated reply hit the system.

In this case, it was about risk management. The stakes are high when a customer is relying on us for accurate and consistent communication. Automating too freely can lead to errors that damage trust.

Are you letting your AI write directly into production, or do you have a review process? What’s your experience?

#AI #Automation #SupportOps #ERP

When I have to explain a technical decision to a non-technical operations owner, it’s a balancing act. I often find that my choice of words matters more than the logic behind the decision itself.

Last week, I pushed back on implementing a seemingly simple customization. The request was straightforward: change how a report looks. But the implications were anything but simple. Modifying that report would affect data integrity across the system. It could lead to confusion in downstream processes, especially if the same data was referenced elsewhere.

I had to explain that while the change would solve an immediate need, it could create a ripple effect in our data structure. That’s when I lean into analogies that relate to their daily operations. I likened it to changing a traffic signal at a busy intersection. It might ease one flow of traffic but could lead to chaos elsewhere.

By framing the decision in a context they understand, I was able to get their buy-in. It turned out to be a valuable lesson: clarity in communication is as crucial as the technical decision itself.

How do you approach explaining complex technical decisions to your operations team?

#Customization #Odoo

One of the most common missteps in Odoo implementations is rushing to install a module. There’s often a temptation to grab the shiny new tool without fully understanding the implications.

I recently had a client who insisted on installing a popular inventory management module. It looked promising on the surface. But once it was live, we hit a wall. The module wasn’t compatible with their existing workflows. Features that were supposed to streamline operations ended up creating additional complexity.

We spent more time fixing the fallout than if we had taken a moment to assess their unique needs. The team ended up frustrated, and the initial excitement was replaced with confusion.

Before installing any module, I now recommend a rigorous evaluation against actual business processes. It’s critical to ensure that what looks good on paper will truly deliver value in practice.

How do you evaluate new modules before installation?
